title: Be Strong and Bold
sum: Moses is dead, and the LORD speaks to Joshua for the first time as leader. He repeats the promise of the land from the wilderness to the Euphrates, promises to be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and three times tells him to be strong and bold (1:1–9). The courage he asks for is above all courage to keep the written law: the "scroll of the law" is to be in Joshua's mouth day and night. Joshua orders the people to prepare to cross in three days (1:10–11), and reminds the eastern tribes, Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, of their promise to fight with their brothers before they settle (1:12–15). They pledge to obey Joshua as they obeyed Moses (1:16–18).
The chapter is almost all speech, and almost every line borrows from Deuteronomy. It works as a bridge: Moses' book closes, and his words carry over into a new leader's hands.
readings: Read as a handover

The chapter is built like an installation ceremony. God speaks to the new leader, the leader speaks to his officials, and the people answer with an oath of loyalty. The same charge, "be strong and bold," is spoken by God (1:6, 7, 9) and then by the people (1:18), so that heaven and earth agree on Joshua.
Read as a sermon on the law

Verses 7–8 shift the meaning of courage from the battlefield to the book. Success depends not on armies but on careful obedience to the written law, read aloud day and night. Many readers see here the key to the whole book: Israel wins when it obeys (chapters 6, 8, 10–11) and loses when it does not (chapter 7).

views.H: Traditional readers see a real transfer of leadership on the plains of Moab in the spring, about forty years after the Exodus, with Joshua now about eighty or older. The words of Deuteronomy are repeated because God is keeping the promises he made through Moses.
views.C: Most critical scholars read chapter 1 as the Deuteronomistic writer's introduction to the conquest, stitched from phrases of Deuteronomy 1–3 and 31. Many see 1:7–8, with its stress on the written law, as an even later layer, since it turns military courage into obedience.
views.E: The ethical problem of the book is already present in the promise: a land that other people live in is "given" to Israel. Readers who wrestle with the conquest often begin with this question of gift and violence, and some note that the promise rests on God's ownership of the whole earth (3:11), not on Israel's merit (Deuteronomy 9:4–6).
views.J: The rabbis drew from 1:8 the duty of constant Torah study. Rabbi Ishmael, asked whether one may study Greek wisdom, answered: find an hour that is neither day nor night (Bavli Menachot 99b). Joshua's role as Moses' disciple is the model of passing on tradition: "Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua" (Mishnah Avot 1:1).
views.X: Christian readers have heard in Joshua's name, Yeshua, a pointer to Jesus, who leads God's people into their inheritance. Hebrews 13:5 applies the promise "I will not let you down" to every believer, and many Christian devotional writers have taken 1:8–9 as a charge for daily life.

deep.b: Nearly every line of 1:1–9 has a source in Deuteronomy. The promise of every place the foot treads and the borders come from Deuteronomy 11:24–25; "no one will be able to stand against you" from 7:24 and 11:25; "I will not let you down, and I will not abandon you" from 31:6 and 31:8; "be strong and bold" from 31:7 and 31:23; the warning not to turn "to the right or to the left" from 5:32 and 17:20; and the scroll of the law from 17:18–19 and 31:24–26. The terms with the eastern tribes in 1:12–15 retell Deuteronomy 3:18–20. The effect is to make Joshua the first person who must live by Deuteronomy as Scripture. Traditional readers see a faithful leader quoting his teacher; critical readers see the hand of the writer who shaped Deuteronomy through Kings.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Joshua as the first reader
deep.b: My own reading, offered as a suggestion: Joshua 1 casts its hero as the Bible's first reader. Before he fights, he is told to keep a book in his mouth. If this is right, the book of Joshua is teaching its own readers how to read: the successes and failures that follow are tests of whether Israel lives by a text. That would help explain why the book ends with Joshua himself writing words "in the book of God's law" (24:26). Many commentators stress the importance of the law in 1:7–8 and 24:26; the idea that the book frames Joshua's life as reading and writing is my own.

echoes: Deuteronomy 3:18–20; Deuteronomy 11:24–25; Deuteronomy 31:6–8; Deuteronomy 31:23; Deuteronomy 34:9; Numbers 32:20–22; Psalm 1:2–3; 1 Chronicles 22:13; Hebrews 4:8; Hebrews 13:5

settings.what: The LORD's charge to Joshua
settings.to: Joshua son of Nun, Moses' assistant, now leader of Israel
settings.when: right after the death of Moses, in the camp at Shittim east of the Jordan
settings.why: God gives Joshua the land from the wilderness to the Euphrates. He promises to be with him as he was with Moses. Three times he tells him to be strong and bold. The courage asked for is above all to keep the written law: "This scroll of the law must not leave your mouth" (1:8). For the book's readers, the scene sets the rule for every leader after Moses: success comes from keeping the law, not from strength.
views: Many critical scholars see the speech as written by the Deuteronomistic editors. They echo Deuteronomy 31:6–8 and Deuteronomy 31:23 almost word for word, to tie Joshua's book to Moses' law.

settings.what: Joshua and the eastern tribes
settings.by: Joshua, and the eastern tribes in answer
settings.to: The fighting men of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, who already had land east of the Jordan
settings.when: before the crossing
settings.why: Joshua reminds the eastern tribes of their promise to Moses (Deuteronomy 3:18–20). They must cross armed ahead of their brothers until all Israel has rest. They pledge to obey Joshua as they obeyed Moses. They end with Moses' own words to him: "Only be strong and bold!" The scene shows one Israel on both sides of the river, a concern that returns in chapter 22.

title: Rahab and the Scarlet Cord
sum: Joshua secretly sends two spies from Shittim to Jericho. They lodge at the house of Rahab, a prostitute, and the king learns of it (2:1–3). Rahab hides them under flax on her roof and sends the king's men off on a false trail (2:4–7). Then she makes a speech of faith: she knows the LORD has given Israel the land, the people of Jericho are melting in fear, and "the LORD your God, he is God in the sky above and on the earth below" (2:8–11). She asks for an oath of loyal love for her family. The spies agree on terms: a scarlet cord in her window, her family inside, her silence kept (2:12–21). They escape to the hills and bring back her words to Joshua (2:22–24).
The first person in the land of promise to confess Israel's God is a Canaanite woman under the ban. The story invites the reader to ask who really belongs to God's people.
readings: Read as a story of faith

Rahab hears about the Exodus and believes, acts on her faith at risk of her life, and is saved with her household. Hebrews 11:31 lists her among the heroes of faith, and James 2:25 pairs her with Abraham as one whose faith worked through deeds.
Read as an ironic tale

The spies are seen at once, hide in a brothel, are saved by a foreign woman's lie and wit, and bring home nothing but her words. Several modern literary readers (Hawk, Nelson) see gentle comedy and a challenge: the outsider is quicker, braver and more faithful than the insiders, and the covenant she wins breaks the strict command of Deuteronomy 7:2.
Read as an Exodus in reverse

Like the Israelites in Egypt on Passover night, Rahab's family must stay inside a house marked with red, and all outside will die. A Canaanite household is spared by the sign, as Israel's houses were spared in Egypt.

views.H: Traditional readers take the story as history: spies did go to Jericho, and Rahab's family lived among Israel. Her house in the wall fits the casemate or wall-backed houses known from some Bronze Age towns.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the Rahab story was once a separate tale, perhaps told by a clan in Israel that traced itself to her (6:25), and later fitted into the conquest account. Her speech (2:9–11) is full of Deuteronomy's phrases and is often assigned to the Deuteronomistic writer.
views.E: Rahab lies to protect life and betrays her own city. Ethicists use her case to discuss whether deception can be right, and whether loyalty to God can justify treason. Her story also shows that the ban was not absolute: a Canaanite who turned to Israel's God lived, which some read as evidence that the conquest stories are about loyalty rather than ethnicity.
views.J: The rabbis counted Rahab among the four most beautiful women in the world and among the righteous converts. They said she married Joshua, and that priests and prophets, including Jeremiah and Huldah, descended from her (Bavli Megillah 14b–15a). The Targum softened her trade to "innkeeper."
views.X: The New Testament names her three times: in Jesus' genealogy as the mother of Boaz (Matthew 1:5), among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:31), and as an example of faith shown in action (James 2:25). From 1 Clement on, Christian writers saw the scarlet cord as a sign of redemption through Christ's blood.

deep.h: Rahab in Jewish and Christian memory
deep.b: Few minor characters have had so long an afterlife. Josephus made her an innkeeper; the Targum followed. The rabbis told that she confessed her sins, praised the God of Israel and became a model of repentance (Bavli Zevachim 116b; Bavli Megillah 15a). For Christians she became a picture of the Gentile church: a sinner from a doomed city, saved by faith, joined to God's people, and written into Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:5). Augustine debated her lie; Calvin judged it a fault covered by grace. In modern times she has been read as a figure of resistance and of the outsider, and also, by some postcolonial critics, as a collaborator whose story justifies conquest.

echoes: Exodus 12:21–23; Exodus 15:14–16; Numbers 13:1–33; Deuteronomy 4:39; Deuteronomy 7:2; Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25; Hosea 2:15

settings.what: Rahab's confession
settings.to: The two Israelite spies hidden on her roof
settings.when: at night, after she has sent the king's men away
settings.why: Rahab says she knows the LORD has given Israel the land. She says he "is God in the sky above and on the earth below" (2:11), the same words Moses used (Deuteronomy 4:39). She asks for an oath of loyal love for her family. The first person in the land to confess Israel's God is a Canaanite woman under the ban. For Israelite readers it shows that an outsider who confesses the LORD can join Israel, as Rahab did (6:25).
views: A convert and a mother of prophets
The rabbis count Rahab among the great converts. The Talmud says eight prophets who were also priests, Jeremiah among them, came from her line (Bavli Megillah 14b).
The New Testament names her in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:5) and praises her faith and deeds (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).

settings.what: The spies' oath, and their report
settings.to: Rahab; then Joshua
settings.when: before she lets them down by a rope from her window, and after three days in the hills
settings.why: The spies swear to spare Rahab and her household on three terms. She must tie a scarlet cord in the window, keep her family inside, and keep silent. The oath bound Israel, and 6:22–25 shows it kept. Back at camp they report that the land has melted with fear. Unlike the scouts of Numbers 13–14, they bring good news, and so undo the earlier generation's failure.

traditions.q: Was Rahab right to lie to save the spies?
views: No. Lying is wrong by its very nature (Catechism 2482–2486), though no one has to tell the truth to someone who has no right to know it (Catechism 2489). Augustine and Thomas Aquinas taught that one may not lie even to save a life, and that Scripture praises Rahab's faith and mercy, not her lie (Augustine, Against Lying; Summa II-II q110 a3).

Many Eastern fathers judged a deception told to protect others more gently. John Chrysostom defended deceiving someone for his own good (On the Priesthood, book 1), and John Cassian, a saint in the Orthodox calendar, counted Rahab's lie as approved because of its purpose (Conferences 17). The Orthodox Church has made no single ruling.

Luther sorted lies into kinds and held that a lie told only to help a neighbor in danger was a useful lie that serves love, not the kind the commandment forbids (Lectures on Genesis). Many later Lutheran teachers have been stricter.

Reformed teachers are divided. Calvin judged that Rahab's lie, though told for a good purpose, was a fault that God pardoned because of her faith (Commentaries on Joshua, on 2:4–6). Charles Hodge argued that deceiving an enemy in war, who has no right to the truth, is not a sinful lie (Systematic Theology, vol. 3).

traditions.q: James says Rahab was justified by works. Are we saved by faith and works together?
views: Justification begins in faith and baptism and grows as faith works through love, so good works done in grace truly share in salvation (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapters 7 and 10; Catechism 1987–1995, 2010). Rahab is a picture of faith that acts.

We are justified by faith alone, for Christ's sake, apart from works (Augsburg Confession 4). James speaks of the works that true faith always produces (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 4). In 1999 Lutherans and Catholics agreed that much of the old quarrel came from using words differently (Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification), though not all Lutherans accept that agreement.

Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone; it always works by love (Westminster Confession 11.2). Calvin read James as showing how faith is proven real, not how a sinner is first made right with God (Institutes 3.17.11–12).

The Orthodox do not frame salvation as faith against works, a debate of the Western churches. Salvation is a lifelong union with God in which God's grace and human effort work together, so Rahab's faith and her deed are one response (Kallistos Ware, The Orthodox Church).

title: The Ark Goes into the River
sum: Israel moves from Shittim to the Jordan's edge and waits three days (3:1–2). The officials tell the people to follow the ark at a distance of two thousand cubits, and Joshua tells them to make themselves holy, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders (3:3–5). God promises to make Joshua great as he made Moses (3:7). Joshua announces the sign: when the priests' feet touch the water, the river will be cut off and stand in a heap, proving that the living God is among them and will drive out the seven nations (3:9–13). It happens as he says. In the spring flood the water stops far upstream at Adam, and the whole nation crosses on dry ground while the priests stand in the riverbed with the ark (3:14–17).
The crossing repeats the Exodus for a new generation and turns a geographical border into a holy threshold.
readings: Read as a second Exodus

The words "heap" and "dry ground" come from the Sea of Reeds (Exodus 14–15). Joshua is a new Moses, the ark replaces the pillar of cloud, and the generation that knew the sea only from stories now has its own crossing. Psalm 114 sings both crossings as one event.
Read as a liturgy

The story reads like a procession: purification, priests, the holy ark, the people following at a set distance, a pause in the riverbed. Many scholars think it was retold at Gilgal in a festival around Passover, and that its repetitions come from liturgical use.

views.H: Traditional readers take the stopping of the river as a real miracle, whether by direct act or by a landslide at Adam timed by God; such blockages are recorded in AD 1267 and 1927.
views.C: Critical scholars generally see the crossing as a story shaped by worship at Gilgal and by the Exodus tradition, with two or more strands woven together, which explains repetitions such as the two sets of stones in chapter 4.
views.E: The chapter's claim that the "living God" will "drive out" seven peoples (3:10) joins wonder and conquest. Some readers note that the first act of the conquest is not violence but a crossing in which God alone acts.
views.J: The rabbis enlarged the miracle, saying the water piled up to an immense height and was seen from afar (Bavli Sotah 34a). They took 3:4 as the source of the 2,000-cubit Sabbath limit.
views.X: Christian writers from Origen on read the crossing of the Jordan as a picture of baptism: Jesus was baptized in the Jordan, and the church's entry into new life follows him through the water. Hymns and spirituals made the Jordan the river of death that the believer crosses into the promised land.

deep.b: Israel camped at Shittim (Abel-shittim) on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan opposite Jericho (Numbers 33:49). The Jordan here runs in a narrow channel through the zor, a floodplain thick with tamarisk, cut some 150 feet below the higher valley floor. Adam (probably Tell ed-Damiyeh) lies about 18 miles north, near where the Jabbok enters the Jordan, and Zarethan somewhere nearby. If the water stopped there, the riverbed downstream would drain within hours, leaving a wide stretch to cross "opposite Jericho." The text stresses that the river was in spring flood (3:15), so the wonder could not be explained by a dry season.

echoes: Exodus 14:21–22; Exodus 15:8; Exodus 19:10–15; Numbers 10:33–36; Psalm 114:1–8; Isaiah 43:2; 2 Kings 2:8; 2 Kings 2:14; Matthew 3:13–17

settings.what: Orders and a sign before the crossing
settings.by: Joshua, and the LORD to Joshua
settings.to: The people of Israel, and the priests who carry the ark
settings.when: at the edge of the Jordan in spring flood
settings.why: Joshua tells the people to make themselves holy, because tomorrow the LORD will do wonders. God promises to make Joshua great as he made Moses. Then Joshua announces the sign. When the priests' feet touch the water, the river will stop. This will prove that the living God is among them and will drive out the nations. The words turn a river crossing into an act of worship, and a new exodus for a new generation.

title: Twelve Stones
sum: Twelve men, one from each tribe, carry stones from the riverbed where the priests stood, and Joshua sets up twelve stones in the river itself (4:1–9). The people hurry across; the eastern tribes go first, armed, about forty thousand of them (4:10–13). On that day the LORD makes Joshua great in Israel's eyes (4:14). At his command the priests come up, and the river returns to its banks (4:15–18). On the tenth day of the first month Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there, telling the people to explain them to their children: Israel crossed on dry ground, as at the Sea of Reeds, so that all peoples would know the LORD's strong hand and Israel would fear him (4:19–24).
The chapter turns an event into a memory that can be handed down. The stones are a sermon for children.
readings: Read as memory-making

The chapter is about how a people remembers. The stones stand where they can be seen, and they are meant to prompt questions. The answer joins the Jordan to the Sea of Reeds, so that every generation's story is part of one story.
Read as a composite

The chapter repeats itself: the crossing is finished twice (4:1, 4:11), the stones are set up twice (4:9, 4:20), the priests come out twice (4:11, 4:18). Many scholars see several accounts woven together; others, like literary critics, see deliberate overlapping and resumption, a way of slowing time at the climax.

views.H: Traditional readers usually take the stones as two memorials, one at Gilgal and one in the riverbed, and the date as exact: the crossing happened four days before Passover, forty years after the Exodus.
views.C: Critical scholars connect the twelve stones with a stone circle at Gilgal, which gave the place its name and was shown to pilgrims; the story explained it. The two sets of stones reflect two traditions.
views.E: The memorial is aimed at "all the peoples of the earth" (4:24), not only Israel. Readers note that the chapter's purpose is knowledge of God, which complicates any reading of the conquest as merely tribal.
views.J: Jewish tradition taught that the stones at Gilgal were the same as those on which the law was written (compare 8:32 and Deuteronomy 27:2–8), and that they were set up on the day of the crossing (Mishnah Sotah 7:5; Bavli Sotah 35b–36a).
views.X: Christian preachers use the stones as a picture of testimony: believers set up "stones" of remembrance when God acts, and teach their children. Some fathers read the twelve stones as the twelve apostles, taken from the river of baptism to build the church.

deep.b: Stones set up as memorials appear often: Jacob's pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), the heap of witness with Laban (Genesis 31:45–48), Moses' twelve pillars at Sinai (Exodus 24:4), Joshua's stone at Shechem (24:26–27), and Samuel's Ebenezer, "stone of help" (1 Samuel 7:12). Deuteronomy forbids sacred pillars as part of Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 16:22), but memorial stones that point to an act of God are treated differently. Archaeologists have found groups of standing stones at many sites in Israel and Jordan, including a shrine at Arad and the large stones at Gezer.

echoes: Exodus 12:26–27; Exodus 14:31; Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 6:20–25; Deuteronomy 27:2–4; Genesis 28:18; 1 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 66:6; Psalm 114:3–5

settings.what: Twelve stones for a sign
settings.to: Twelve men, one from each tribe, chosen to carry stones from the riverbed
settings.when: while the priests stand in the Jordan
settings.why: Each man carries a stone from where the priests stood. The stones are a sign. When children ask what they mean, their parents can tell them the river was cut off before the ark. The words look ahead to later generations.

settings.what: What to tell your children about the stones
settings.to: The Israelites encamped at Gilgal, as parents of children to come
settings.when: on the tenth day of the first month, at Gilgal
settings.why: Joshua gives parents the answer to their children's question. Israel crossed on dry ground, as at the Sea of Reeds. It happened so that all peoples would know the LORD's strong hand, and Israel would fear him. Like Deuteronomy 6:20–25, the speech makes each household a place where the story is handed down. For later readers who passed the stones at Gilgal, it was their own lesson.

title: Circumcision, Passover and a Holy Place
sum: The kings of Canaan lose heart when they hear of the crossing (5:1). At God's command Joshua makes flint knives and circumcises the generation born in the wilderness, since their fathers who left Egypt had died without circumcising them (5:2–7). The people stay in camp until they heal, and God says, "Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt," which gives Gilgal its name (5:8–9). Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth of the month and eats the produce of the land; the next day the manna stops (5:10–12). Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword, who says he is the commander of the LORD's army. Joshua falls on his face and is told to take off his sandal, for the ground is holy (5:13–15).
Before any battle, Israel is marked again as God's covenant people: circumcised, fed by the land, and standing on holy ground.
readings: Read as covenant renewal

The three scenes each restore something from the Exodus: the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17), the Passover meal (Exodus 12), and an encounter at holy ground like the burning bush (Exodus 3). The wilderness is over; the land begins.
Read as risk and trust

Circumcising the whole army in enemy territory, days before a siege, is militarily foolish. Readers compare Genesis 34, where Simeon and Levi exploited the men of Shechem's pain. Israel makes itself weak on purpose and trusts God to protect it.

views.H: Traditional readers see a literal mass circumcision and Passover at Gilgal in spring, with the commander of the army as an angel or a pre-incarnate appearance of the Word of God.
views.C: Critical scholars note that the circumcision story explains two names, the Hill of Foreskins and Gilgal, and that the Septuagint tells 5:4–6 quite differently. Many see the commander's visit as a fragment whose message has been lost or moved to 6:2–5.
views.E: The commander's answer, "No," to the question "Are you for us?" is often cited by ethicists: God is not simply on Israel's side, and the conquest is not a blank check. The same book will show God fighting against Israel at Ai.
views.J: The Talmud says the commander came to rebuke Israel for neglecting Torah study (Bavli Megillah 3a). Many Jewish interpreters identified him as Michael. The rabbis explained the "second" circumcision as the completion of the rite with peri'ah (Bavli Yevamot 71b).
views.X: Paul speaks of a circumcision "not made with hands" in Christ (Colossians 2:11), and Justin Martyr saw Joshua's second circumcision with stone knives as a type of Jesus' circumcision of the heart. Many Christians read the commander as Christ, since Joshua bows down before him (the same Hebrew word as worship) and is told the ground is holy, honor angels elsewhere refuse (Revelation 22:8–9).

deep.h: Who was circumcised in the wilderness?
deep.b: The Hebrew text says that all who left Egypt were circumcised but those born in the wilderness were not (5:5). Why would Moses' generation neglect it? Readers have suggested that the hardships of travel made it dangerous; that the generation under judgment (Numbers 14) was not allowed the covenant sign for its children; or, with the rabbis, that the north wind did not blow in the wilderness and so wounds would not heal (Bavli Yevamot 71b–72a). The Septuagint tells it differently: some who came out of Egypt were uncircumcised too, and the wandering lasted forty-two years (see the variants at 5:4 and 5:6).

echoes: Genesis 17:9–14; Genesis 34:24–25; Exodus 3:1–6; Exodus 4:24–26; Exodus 12:43–49; Exodus 16:35; Numbers 14:29–35; Numbers 22:31; Colossians 2:11–12

settings.what: Circumcision at Gilgal: the disgrace rolled away
settings.to: Joshua, and through him the sons of the wilderness generation, at Gilgal
settings.when: after the crossing, before the first Passover in the land
settings.why: God tells Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise the Israelites a second time. The men born in the wilderness had never been circumcised. When it is done, God declares that the disgrace of Egypt is rolled away, which gives Gilgal its name. The command marks the new generation as the covenant people before the Passover (Exodus 12:48) and before any battle. It also explains a place name the readers knew.

settings.what: The commander of the LORD's army
settings.by: A man with a drawn sword, the commander of the LORD's army
settings.to: Joshua, alone near Jericho
settings.when: before the attack on Jericho
settings.why: Joshua asks whether the man is for Israel or its enemies. He answers "No." He has come as commander of the LORD's army. Joshua must take off his sandal, as Moses did at the bush (Exodus 3:5). The scene tells readers that the war is the LORD's, and Israel does not own God.

title: The Walls Fall
sum: Jericho is shut tight. God gives Joshua the strange plan: for six days the army, seven priests with ram's horns, and the ark march once around the town in silence except for the horns; on the seventh day they march seven times, and at the long blast the people shout and the wall falls (6:1–16). The town is to be put under the ban for the LORD: everyone killed except Rahab's household, and the metals given to the LORD's treasury (6:17–19). It happens as promised. The wall collapses, Israel takes the town and kills all who are in it (6:20–21). The two spies bring Rahab and her family out to safety (6:22–25). Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds Jericho (6:26), and his fame spreads (6:27).
The most famous battle of the book is hardly a battle at all, and it ends with the hardest command in the book.
readings: Read as worship
The "battle" is a seven-day procession led by priests and the ark, with horns and a shout. God wins the victory; Israel's part is to obey and to praise. Hebrews 11:30 says the walls fell "by faith."
Read as a first fruits offering
Jericho is the first town taken, and like the first fruits of the harvest it belongs wholly to God. That explains why nothing may be kept and why taking anything is so serious (chapter 7).
Read with discomfort

Many modern readers cannot read 6:21 without thinking of real massacres. They ask how the God who spares Rahab can command the death of children, and whether the text is history, hyperbole or ideology. The book itself places the killing beside the rescue of a Canaanite family.

views.H: Traditional readers take the fall of the walls as a miracle, possibly aided by an earthquake, and point to Garstang's and Wood's work at Jericho. They hold that the ban was a unique judgment on peoples whose sin was "full" (Genesis 15:16).
views.C: Most archaeologists follow Kenyon in finding no walled town at Jericho in the late 13th century BC. Critical scholars read the story as a liturgical tale or an etiology explaining the ruins, written centuries later.
views.E: Nicholas Wolterstorff, Paul Copan and others argue that "every man and woman" is a stock phrase of ancient war reports and not a literal record; Eric Seibert and Gregory Boyd argue that Christians must read such texts critically in light of Jesus; Native American and Palestinian readers have described how the story was used to justify the taking of their lands.
views.J: The rabbis said Jericho was taken on a Sabbath, and debated how the march could be allowed. Jewish tradition held that Joshua had offered peace before the war (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 6:1), and Maimonides ruled that peace must be offered even to the seven nations (Laws of Kings 6:1).
views.X: Hebrews 11:30–31 holds up both the walls and Rahab as examples of faith. Origen read the priests' trumpets as the apostles' preaching, at which the walls of the world fall. Revelation's seven trumpets that bring down a great city echo this chapter.

deep.b: John Garstang (1930–1936) found a collapsed double wall and burned town he dated to about 1400 BC. Kathleen Kenyon (1952–1958) showed that the collapsed wall belonged to the Early Bronze Age, a thousand years earlier, and that the last great walled town (City IV) was destroyed about 1550 BC, probably by Egyptians driving out the Hyksos; she found only a little 14th-century material and nothing that could be a 13th-century town. Bryant Wood (1990) argued from pottery and a scarab sequence that City IV fell about 1400 BC, fitting the biblical early date; Piotr Bienkowski and most others disagreed, and radiocarbon tests on charred grain (1995) gave dates near 1560 BC. An Italian-Palestinian team led by Lorenzo Nigro and Nicolò Marchetti has worked at the site since 1997 and confirmed the Middle Bronze destruction. The debate goes on, but the majority view is that Jericho was a ruin or a small unwalled settlement when most scholars place Israel's arrival.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a battle shaped like a week
deep.b: Seven days, with the seventh different, ending in a great shout and a fall, is the shape of the creation week and of Israel's festivals. I suggest that the Jericho story is told as a holy week, so that Israel's first act in the land is to keep God's time: six days of going around, then a seventh day on which God, not Israel, does the work. If so, the old rabbinic tradition that Jericho fell on a Sabbath touches the story's own design. Scholars widely note the sevens; the link to the Sabbath pattern is my own suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24–28; Leviticus 27:28–29; Numbers 21:2–3; Deuteronomy 7:1–6; Deuteronomy 20:16–18; 1 Samuel 15:3; 1 Kings 16:34; Wisdom 12:3–11; Hebrews 11:30–31; Revelation 8:2–6

settings.what: The LORD's plan for Jericho
settings.to: Joshua
settings.when: before the march around Jericho
settings.why: God gives a strange plan. Israel must march around the town for six days, and seven times on the seventh, with priests blowing ram's horns before the ark. Then they must shout. The victory will be God's, won by worship and obedience, not by siege.

settings.what: Joshua's orders for the march
settings.to: The priests who carry the ark and the horns, and the people and armed men
settings.when: on the first day of the march
settings.why: Joshua passes on the plan and orders silence until the day he says "Shout!" The people's obedience, day after day, is the test.

settings.what: The ban on Jericho
settings.to: The people of Israel on the seventh day
settings.when: just before the shout
settings.why: Joshua puts the town under the ban: everything in it is the LORD's. Only Rahab and her household live. The silver, gold, bronze and iron go into the LORD's treasury. The command sets up the story of Achan in chapter 7. For readers, it is among the hardest commands in the Bible.
views: Traditional readers take the ban as a real command limited to the towns of Canaan in that war.
Younger and others show that ancient conquest reports regularly speak of total destruction in stylized terms. The same book later says many Canaanites remained (13:13; 15:63).
Earl and others read the ban, for later Israel, as a call to give up everything to God and to purge idolatry.

settings.what: Joshua's curse on the rebuilder of Jericho
settings.to: The people of Israel, who take the oath with him
settings.when: after Jericho falls
settings.why: Anyone who rebuilds Jericho will lay its foundation at the cost of his firstborn. He will set up its gates at the cost of his youngest. The curse makes the ruin a lasting witness. 1 Kings 16:34 tells of Hiel of Bethel, who rebuilt it under Ahab and lost two sons.

title: Trouble in the Camp
sum: The chapter opens by telling the reader what Israel does not know: Achan of Judah has taken some of what was under the ban, and the LORD is angry (7:1). Spies advise sending only a few thousand men against little Ai; they are routed and thirty-six are killed, and Israel's heart melts (7:2–5). Joshua and the elders lie before the ark in mourning, and Joshua asks why God brought them over the Jordan at all (7:6–9). God tells him to get up: Israel has sinned and broken the covenant, and he will not be with them until the banned things are removed (7:10–15). By lot, tribe by tribe, clan by clan, the guilty man is found. Achan confesses that he saw, craved and took a robe, silver and gold (7:16–21). The goods are found, and Achan and all he has are stoned and burned in the Valley of Achor, "Trouble" (7:22–26).
After the triumph of Jericho, the book's first defeat comes from within. One man's hidden sin is treated as the whole people's.
readings: Read as the mirror of Rahab

Rahab the Canaanite hid the spies, confessed the LORD, and was saved with her household. Achan the Judahite hid stolen goods, confessed too late, and died with his household. Belonging to Israel is a matter of loyalty to God, not of birth.
Read as a lesson on holiness

Things under the ban belong to God and are dangerous to hold, like the holy things of the sanctuary. Achan's theft makes Israel itself "something under the ban" (7:12). The chapter teaches that the holy is not to be handled lightly, as with Nadab and Abihu or Uzzah (Leviticus 10:1–3; 2 Samuel 6:6–7).
Read as a hard case

Readers have long been troubled that Achan's sons and daughters seem to die with him, against Deuteronomy 24:16, and that thirty-six men die at Ai for one man's sin. Some take this as the cost of a covenant in which the community is one body; others see a text whose violence must be faced honestly.

views.H: Traditional readers take the story as history and as a moral lesson: sin hidden in the camp brings defeat, and confession honors God. Many explain the family's death by their knowledge of the hidden loot.
views.C: Critical scholars read the chapter as a story explaining the name of the Valley of Achor and the heap of stones there, joined to the Ai story. The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 2:7 call him Achar, matching the pun.
views.E: The chapter raises the problem of collective punishment. Ethicists point out that the Bible itself later rejects punishing children for parents (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18), and debate whether the story reflects a different moral world or a special holiness law.
views.J: The rabbis taught that Achan's confession won him a share in the world to come, and that "this day" in 7:25 limited his punishment to this world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:2). From "Israel has sinned" they drew the principle that a Jew who sins is still a Jew (Bavli Sanhedrin 44a).
views.X: Christian writers have compared Achan to Ananias and Sapphira, who kept back part of what was dedicated and died (Acts 5:1–11), and used the story to teach about the effect of hidden sin on a church (1 Corinthians 5:6). Hosea's promise of the Valley of Achor as "a door of hope" has been read as fulfilled in Christ.

deep.h: Lots, confession and the Valley of Achor
deep.b: The process of selection (7:14–18) slowly narrows the field, which gives the guilty man every chance to come forward. Joshua's words to Achan are gentle, "my son," and he asks for a confession that will "give glory to the LORD." Achan's confession uses the same three verbs as the first sin in Eden: saw, craved, took. The place of his death, the Valley of Achor, is remembered in the prophets as a place that God will turn into a door of hope (Hosea 2:15) and a pasture (Isaiah 65:10). Archaeologists usually place it in the Buqei'a, a plain above the Dead Sea where Iron Age farms and forts have been found.

echoes: Genesis 3:6; Exodus 20:17; Leviticus 27:28–29; Deuteronomy 7:25–26; Deuteronomy 13:16–17; Deuteronomy 24:16; 1 Chronicles 2:7; Hosea 2:15; Isaiah 65:10; Acts 5:1–11

settings.what: The scouts' report on Ai
settings.by: The men Joshua sent to spy out Ai
settings.to: Joshua, at Jericho
settings.when: after the fall of Jericho
settings.why: The scouts tell Joshua not to send all the people, because the people of Ai are few; two or three thousand men will do. Their confident report is the opposite of the fear of Numbers 13. But readers already know from 7:1 that Achan has broken the ban. The advice sets up the defeat, and shows Israel trusting its own strength without asking the LORD.

settings.what: Joshua's lament after Ai
settings.to: The LORD, before the ark, with the elders mourning beside him
settings.when: after thirty-six men die at Ai
settings.why: Joshua asks why God brought Israel across the Jordan only to be destroyed. He asks what God will do for his great name. The prayer echoes the people's complaints in the wilderness, but also Moses' appeal to God's name (Numbers 14:13–16).

settings.what: The LORD's answer: Israel has sinned
settings.to: Joshua
settings.when: while Joshua lies on his face before the ark
settings.why: God tells Joshua to get up: Israel has broken the covenant by taking what was under the ban. The guilty one will be found by lot. The answer shows readers that one person's hidden sin can bring disaster on the whole people.

settings.what: Achan's confession and sentence
settings.by: Achan son of Carmi, of Judah, and Joshua
settings.to: Joshua, before all Israel; then Achan, in the Valley of Achor
settings.when: after the lot falls on him
settings.why: Achan confesses that he saw, wanted and took a fine cloak, silver and gold, and hid them in his tent. The same three steps, seeing, wanting, taking, are Eve's in Genesis 3:6. The confession is the warning: an Israelite of the leading tribe falls, while the Canaanite Rahab is saved. Joshua's sentence, "Why have you brought trouble on us?", plays on the name Achor, Trouble. It explains to later readers the stone heap there "to this day."

title: Ambush at Ai, Blessing at Ebal
sum: God encourages Joshua again and gives him the plan: set an ambush behind Ai, and this time Israel may keep the livestock and plunder (8:1–2). Joshua places thousands of men in hiding west of the town, between Ai and Bethel, and leads the main army openly from the north (8:3–13). The king of Ai attacks, Israel pretends to flee, and all the men of Ai and Bethel pour out after them (8:14–17). At God's word Joshua holds out his javelin; the ambush takes and burns the town, and the men of Ai are caught between two armies (8:18–23). Twelve thousand die, Ai becomes a ruin mound, and the king's body hangs on a tree until evening (8:24–29). Then Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes the law on stones, and reads all of it to the whole people, women, children and foreigners included, with half the tribes before Gerizim and half before Ebal (8:30–35).
Defeat is reversed, and the conquest pauses for worship. The scene at Ebal fulfills Deuteronomy 27 to the letter.
readings: Read as restoration

The same town that beat Israel when God was absent falls when God is present. God speaks first this time, and Joshua obeys. The outstretched javelin recalls Moses' raised hands against Amalek: the victory is God's.
Read as covenant renewal

Placed after the first victories, the Ebal ceremony makes the land itself a place of covenant. Israel writes and reads the law in the very heart of the land, and the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy are spoken where Abraham first built an altar (Genesis 12:6–7).

views.H: Traditional readers take the ambush as a real battle at Ai (some proposing Khirbet el-Maqatir instead of et-Tell) and the Ebal ceremony as a march to Shechem soon after, perhaps through friendly or frightened country. Some link Zertal's structure on Ebal with Joshua's altar.
views.C: Most critical scholars read the Ai story as an etiology of the ruins at et-Tell, which were empty in the late Bronze Age. They see 8:30–35 as a later insertion, as its three different positions in the Hebrew, the Greek and 4QJosh-a show.
views.E: The ban at Ai includes "men and women" (8:25), and the king's body is hung up as a public example. Some readers note that, unlike at Jericho, Israel may keep the plunder, which suggests the ban was not a fixed ritual but varied by command.
views.J: The Mishnah describes the ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim in detail: the Levites stood in the valley facing Gerizim to bless and Ebal to curse, and the people answered "Amen" (Mishnah Sotah 7:5). The rabbis taught that the law was written on the stones in seventy languages.
views.X: Christian readers note that the law is read to everyone, including foreigners, a sign of the gospel's reach. The hanging of the king and the burial at sunset are linked by Paul's reading of Deuteronomy 21:23 about Christ hanging on a tree (Galatians 3:13).

deep.h: Why Ebal, the mountain of the curse?
deep.b: Deuteronomy commands the altar and the written stones on Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 27:4), the mountain on which the curses were spoken (Deuteronomy 27:13), not on Gerizim, the mountain of blessing. The Samaritan Pentateuch reads "Gerizim" in Deuteronomy 27:4, and a few scholars think that was the original reading, changed in the Jewish text because of the Samaritan temple on Gerizim. An Old Latin manuscript also has "Gerizim." So does a small fragment published in 2009, but it has no known find-site, and it belongs to a group of market fragments widely judged to be modern forgeries (Davis and others, 2017). Others think Ebal was original and the Samaritans changed it. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have taken the altar on the mountain of the curse as a sign that sacrifice deals with the curse. See the topic on Shechem.

echoes: Deuteronomy 11:29–30; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Deuteronomy 27:1–26; Deuteronomy 31:10–13; Exodus 17:9–13; Exodus 20:24–26; Genesis 12:6–7; 2 Kings 23:1–3; Nehemiah 8:1–8; Galatians 3:13

settings.what: The LORD's plan and Joshua's orders for Ai
settings.to: Joshua; then thirty thousand chosen fighters sent out by night
settings.when: after Achan's punishment
settings.why: God tells Joshua not to fear, and to set an ambush. This time Israel may keep the livestock and the plunder. Joshua passes the plan to his men: hide behind the town, wait while the main army draws the defenders out, then take it and burn it. He ends, "Do as the LORD has said." The words restore the people after defeat and show the victory coming by obedience.

settings.what: The law read at Mount Ebal
settings.to: The whole assembly of Israel, with the women, the children and the foreigners who lived among them, on Mounts Ebal and Gerizim
settings.when: after the fall of Ai, as Moses had commanded (Deuteronomy 27:1–8)
settings.why: Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and writes a copy of the law on stones. He reads every word of it to all the people, with the blessings and the curses. Half stand facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal. It carries out Moses' command and shows Israel taking the covenant into the land. For later readers, it is a model of a public reading of the law to everyone, including the foreigner.
views: The scene sits oddly here. The Septuagint puts it after 9:2. A Dead Sea Scroll (4QJosh-a) seems to put it right after the crossing, at Gilgal. Many scholars think it was moved.
Critical scholars compare Josiah reading the scroll to all the people and making a covenant (2 Kings 23:1–3).

title: The Gibeonite Trick
sum: The kings west of the Jordan unite to fight Israel (9:1–2). But the people of Gibeon choose another way. They dress in worn-out clothes and sandals, load their donkeys with cracked wineskins and crumbling bread, and come to Gilgal claiming to be from a far country (9:3–6). Israel's men suspect them, but the visitors tell of the Exodus and of Sihon and Og, and show their stale bread (9:7–13). Israel tastes their food but does not ask the LORD; Joshua makes peace with them, and the leaders swear an oath (9:14–15). Three days later the truth comes out: Gibeon and its three towns are close by. The community grumbles, but the leaders will not break their oath (9:16–21). Joshua curses the Gibeonites to serve as woodcutters and water carriers for the house of God, and they accept, saying they acted from fear of the LORD's command (9:22–27).
A second Canaanite group escapes the ban, this time by a lie that uses Deuteronomy's own rules. Israel keeps its word, even when tricked.
readings: Read as a failure

The narrator's judgment is plain: "they did not ask the LORD what to do" (9:14). Israel trusted its eyes and its stomach, and broke Deuteronomy 7:2. The covenant with Gibeon will drag Israel into war (chapter 10) and later bring famine (2 Samuel 21).
Read as grace

Like Rahab, the Gibeonites hear of the LORD's acts, fear him and seek life from his people. Their words echo hers (9:9–10, 24). They end up serving at God's altar. Some readers see the story as quietly approving of Canaanites who seek peace, even if their means were wrong.

views.H: Traditional readers take the Gibeonite league as historical, pointing to Gibeon's later role as a Hivite enclave and a priestly town, and to the famine under David caused by Saul's breach of the oath.
views.C: Critical scholars often see the story as explaining why non-Israelites served at an Israelite sanctuary, perhaps at Gibeon's own high place or later at the temple. Some think it preserves a memory of a real treaty between early Israel and the Gibeonite towns.
views.E: The story shows an oath kept even when it was obtained by fraud, and a people spared from the ban. Some ethicists see a crack in the conquest ideology: the ban gives way to a sworn word. Others note the cost to the Gibeonites, made permanent menial workers.
views.J: The Talmud explains that the oath was kept for the sake of God's name (Bavli Gittin 46a), and records that David barred the Gibeonites from marrying into Israel because of their cruelty to Saul's descendants (Bavli Yevamot 78b–79a). Jewish tradition taught that Joshua had offered the Canaanites a choice: leave, make peace, or fight (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 6:1).
views.X: Christian moralists used the story to teach that oaths must be kept even to enemies. Some fathers saw the Gibeonites as a picture of Gentiles who come in humility and serve in God's house.

deep.h: How the Gibeonites knew the law
deep.b: The Gibeonites' speech is carefully chosen. They claim a "far country," the category Deuteronomy 20:15 allows Israel to make peace with. They mention the Exodus and the victories over Sihon and Og, but not Jericho and Ai, which a truly distant people could not have heard of yet. And they confess at the end that they knew "the LORD your God commanded his servant Moses to give you the whole land and to wipe out all who live in the land" (9:24). In other words, they understood Israel's law better than Israel's leaders did in the moment. Literary readers (Hawk, Nelson) see sharp irony here; the people who were meant to be destroyed survive by reading Deuteronomy closely.

echoes: Exodus 23:32; Exodus 34:12; Deuteronomy 7:1–2; Deuteronomy 20:10–18; Deuteronomy 29:11; 2 Samuel 21:1–14; 1 Kings 3:4–5; 1 Chronicles 9:2; Nehemiah 3:7; Ezra 2:43

settings.what: The Gibeonites' story
settings.to: Joshua and the men of Israel at the camp at Gilgal
settings.when: after the fall of Jericho and Ai
settings.why: The Gibeonites, in worn-out clothes and with dry bread, claim to come from a far country. They ask for a treaty. Their speech uses Israel's own story of Egypt and of Sihon and Og. It works because Israel does not ask the LORD. For readers, it explains why the Gibeonites lived among Israel and served at the sanctuary.

settings.what: The leaders' ruling: the oath holds
settings.to: The whole community, grumbling against them
settings.when: three days after the treaty, when the trick is found out
settings.why: "We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, so now we cannot touch them" (9:19). An oath in the LORD's name holds even when it was won by a trick, because breaking it would bring anger on Israel. The Gibeonites live, and serve as woodcutters and water carriers. The ruling explains to later readers why Gibeon lived among Israel, and 2 Samuel 21:1–9 shows the oath still binding under Saul and David.

settings.what: Joshua's curse and the Gibeonites' answer
settings.by: Joshua, and the Gibeonites in answer
settings.to: The people of Gibeon
settings.when: three days after the treaty, when the trick is found out
settings.why: Joshua curses them to be woodcutters and water carriers for the house of God. They answer that they feared for their lives, because they heard what the LORD commanded Moses. Their answer is a kind of confession, like Rahab's.

traditions.q: Israel kept its oath to Gibeon. May Christians swear oaths?
views: Yes, for a serious reason such as a court, since an oath calls God to witness the truth (Catechism 2154). Jesus' words against swearing (Matthew 5:33–37) forbid careless and false oaths, not every oath.
Yes. The Thirty-Nine Articles (article 39) teach that Christians may swear when a magistrate requires it, if it is done in justice, judgment and truth.
A lawful oath is a part of worship, and it must be kept even when keeping it costs, as Israel kept its word to Gibeon (Westminster Confession 22). But no oath can bind anyone to sin.
No. The Schleitheim Confession (article 7) holds that Christ forbids all swearing, so his followers answer only yes or no. Many Mennonites and Amish still affirm rather than swear in court.
No. Robert Barclay argued that Christ's words end all swearing (Apology, proposition 15), and early Quakers went to prison rather than take oaths, until English law let them affirm instead.

title: The Day the Sun Stood Still
sum: Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem gathers four other Amorite kings to punish Gibeon for its treaty (10:1–5). Gibeon calls for help, and Joshua marches all night from Gilgal (10:6–9). The LORD throws the enemy into panic; Israel chases them down the pass of Beth-horon, and great hailstones kill more than Israel's swords (10:10–11). Joshua speaks to the LORD and commands the sun and moon to stand still, quoting a song from the Book of Jashar; the sun stays in the sky about a whole day, and there has never been a day like it (10:12–15). The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah; Joshua's men seal it, finish the battle, then bring the kings out, put their feet on their necks, kill them and hang them on trees until evening (10:16–27). Joshua then takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron and Debir, leaving no survivors, and the summary claims the whole south from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza (10:28–43).
Israel's new ally pulls it into its biggest battle, and the chapter contains the Bible's most famous cosmic miracle.
readings: Read as a literal miracle

Many Jewish and Christian readers through the centuries have taken the sun's standing still as a real halt in the heavens. The debate over this verse played a part in the Galileo affair, when church officials cited it against the idea that the earth moves.
Read as poetry and annals

The quotation in 10:12–13 is a short poem from a lost song book. Read as poetry, it may describe the length and greatness of the day in figurative terms, as Judges 5:20 says the stars fought from heaven. The rest of the chapter reads like an ancient war report, with stock formulas repeated town by town.

views.H: Traditional readers take the campaign as historical and the long day as a real miracle, though explained in various ways: a halt of the earth's rotation, a prolonged light, or (for some evangelical scholars) a darkening or an eclipse.
views.C: Critical scholars see the chapter as a composite: an old poem (10:12–13), stories tied to landmarks (the cave at Makkedah, 10:27), and a formulaic list of conquests in Deuteronomy's style. They note that Hebron, Debir and Jerusalem appear later in Canaanite hands.
views.E: The hanging of the kings, the feet on their necks, and "he left no survivor" make this one of the book's grimmest chapters. Readers who see the language as hyperbole point to the later chapters where the same towns must be taken again.
views.J: The Talmud counts Joshua among three for whom the sun stood still, with Moses and Nakdimon ben Gurion (Bavli Avodah Zarah 25a; Bavli Taanit 20a), and asks what the Book of Jashar is. Medieval commentators such as Gersonides suggested the miracle was that Israel's victory came so fast, before the sun moved far.
views.X: Habakkuk 3:11 recalls the sun and moon standing still in God's battle. Christian commentators from Augustine on have seen in Joshua's prayer an example of faith, and Luther and Calvin defended a literal halt. The Galileo controversy (1610s–1630s) made this verse famous in the history of science.

deep.b: When Copernicus argued that the earth moves around the sun, Joshua 10:12–13 became a key text in the debate. Luther is reported to have said at table that "Joshua commanded the sun to stand still, not the earth." In 1615 Galileo answered in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina that the Bible speaks in the language of ordinary appearance and that the verse actually fits the new astronomy better. The Roman Inquisition condemned heliocentrism in 1616 and tried Galileo in 1633. Most Christians and Jews today, including those who hold to a real miracle, agree that the text describes what was seen from the ground, as we still speak of "sunrise."

The verse quotes a poetic collection, the Book of Jashar, which is also cited for David's lament (2 Samuel 1:18). It shows that biblical writers used older written sources and expected readers to know them. The book is lost; later works under that name are medieval or modern compositions.

echoes: Exodus 14:14; Exodus 14:24–25; Exodus 23:27; Deuteronomy 7:24; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Judges 1:5–7; Judges 5:20; 2 Samuel 1:18; Psalm 110:1; Isaiah 28:21; Psalm 44:1–3; Habakkuk 3:11; Sirach 46:4–6

settings.what: Joshua's command to the sun and moon
settings.by: Joshua, speaking to the LORD in the sight of Israel
settings.to: The LORD, and the sun over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon
settings.when: during the battle at Beth-horon
settings.why: Joshua commands the sun to stand still, quoting a song from the Book of Jashar. The narrator says there was never a day like it, "when the LORD listened to a man's voice, for the LORD fought for Israel" (10:14). For readers, the point is not astronomy but that the LORD fights for his people.
views: Traditional readers take the sun's stopping as a real miracle.
Many read the quoted poem as a prayer for a good omen, in the language of Mesopotamian omen texts (Walton). Others suggest an eclipse.

settings.what: Feet on the kings' necks
settings.to: The commanders of Israel's fighting men
settings.when: at the cave of Makkedah, with the five kings brought out
settings.why: Joshua has the commanders put their feet on the kings' necks. He tells them, "Be strong and bold," for the LORD will do this to all their enemies. He passes on to his officers the courage God gave him in 1:9.

title: Hazor and the North
sum: Jabin king of Hazor gathers the kings of the north, a host like the sand of the sea with many horses and chariots, at the waters of Merom (11:1–5). God tells Joshua not to fear and to hamstring their horses and burn their chariots. Joshua attacks suddenly and chases them as far as Sidon (11:6–9). He takes Hazor, the head of all those kingdoms, kills its people and burns it; the other towns on their mounds are taken but not burned (11:10–15). The chapter then sums up: Joshua took the whole land, from the Negev to Mount Hermon, after a long war; no town except Gibeon made peace, because the LORD hardened their hearts (11:16–20). He destroyed the Anakim from the hill country, leaving some only in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (11:21–22). Joshua took the whole land and gave it to Israel as an inheritance, and the land was quiet from war (11:23).
The northern campaign mirrors the southern one, and the summary closes the first half of the book with the promise apparently fulfilled.
readings: Read as fulfillment

The last verses of chapter 11 repeat "all the land" and "as the LORD commanded Moses" again and again. The point is that God kept his word: the land promised in 1:3–4 is now in Israel's hand, and Joshua has done everything Moses commanded (11:15).
Read with chapter 13

Two chapters later God says "very much of the land" remains (13:1). Read together, the two claims show the gap between the completeness of God's gift and the slowness of Israel's possession, a gap the book of Judges will explore.

views.H: Traditional readers see a historical northern campaign and point to the great 13th-century destruction of Hazor, though those holding a 15th-century date must explain why the clearest destruction is later.
views.C: Many archaeologists accept that Hazor was destroyed in the 13th century BC, but debate who did it. Critical scholars note the overlap with Judges 4–5, where Jabin of Hazor is still ruling, and see the summary statements as Deuteronomistic idealization.
views.E: 11:20 says the LORD hardened the Canaanites' hearts so they would not seek mercy. Ethicists find this one of the most troubling verses, since it seems to make God responsible for their refusal. Others read it alongside Rahab and Gibeon, who did seek peace.
views.J: The rabbis held that Joshua sent three letters to the Canaanites before the war, offering peace or departure, and that the Girgashites left for Africa (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 6:1; Leviticus Rabbah 17:6). On this reading, those who fought had chosen to.
views.X: Christian readers have used 11:20 in discussions of divine sovereignty alongside Pharaoh and Romans 9. The burning of chariots has been read as a lesson against trusting in power, and "the land was quiet" as a foretaste of the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4).

deep.b: Hazor was the largest city of Bronze Age Canaan, with an upper city of about 30 acres and a lower city of some 170 acres. It is named in Egyptian execration texts, in the Mari archives of the 18th century BC, and in the Amarna letters of the 14th century BC. Yigael Yadin excavated it in 1955–1958 and 1968, and Amnon Ben-Tor has led excavations since 1990. Both found that the last Canaanite city ended in a fierce fire in the 13th century BC, with temple statues deliberately broken, and both argued that early Israelites were the likeliest attackers. The city was later rebuilt by Solomon and fortified by Ahab (1 Kings 9:15).

echoes: Exodus 4:21; Exodus 23:29–30; Deuteronomy 2:30; Deuteronomy 7:22; Deuteronomy 17:16; Judges 4:2; Judges 4:23–24; 2 Samuel 8:4; Psalm 20:7; Amos 2:9; Romans 9:17–18

settings.what: Do not be afraid of the northern kings
settings.to: Joshua, facing the kings of the north at the waters of Merom
settings.why: God promises victory and commands Joshua to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots. Israel must not trust in horses, as the law of the king also warns (Deuteronomy 17:16).

title: Thirty-One Kings
sum: The first half of the book ends with a list. First come the two kings defeated under Moses east of the Jordan: Sihon of Heshbon, whose land ran from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and Og of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim. Moses gave their land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh (12:1–6). Then come the kings Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the north to Mount Halak in the south: thirty-one kings in all, from Jericho and Ai to Megiddo, Hazor and Tirzah, each counted as "one" (12:7–24).
The list turns the stories of chapters 2–11 into a record, and joins Moses' victories with Joshua's as one conquest.
readings: Read as a victory record
Like the lists of conquered towns carved by Egyptian pharaohs, the chapter is a monument in words. It names kings rather than towns, because the war was against rulers and their power.
Read as a bridge

The list looks back on what was taken and forward to the division of the land (chapters 13–21). By starting with the eastern tribes' land, it also prepares for the problem of chapter 22: are those across the Jordan truly part of Israel?

views.H: Traditional readers take the list as an official record, noting that it includes towns whose capture is not narrated, which suggests a fuller source than the stories.
views.C: Critical scholars see the list as a later compilation, perhaps reflecting the extent of Israel's kingdom under David or the north under its kings. Several towns, such as Gezer, Megiddo and Taanach, stayed Canaanite according to Judges 1 and 1 Kings 9:16.
views.E: A list of defeated kings is a list of wars. Some readers note that the list counts rulers, not peoples, which fits the view that the conquest was aimed at Canaan's city-states and their kings.
views.J: The Talmud rules that this list, like the list of Haman's sons, is written in a scroll in stacked columns, a special layout for the downfall of the wicked (Bavli Megillah 16b). Jewish commentators also noted how many of these towns reappear later in Canaanite hands, and read the list as the defeat of kings, not the settlement of land.
views.X: Christian readers have used the list as a picture of complete victory over every power that opposes God, though few have made much of it. Its main role for them is historical: the God who promised is the God who kept his word.

deep.b: Many of the names are major sites known to archaeology: Megiddo and Taanach guard the Jezreel Valley; Aphek lies on the coastal road; Tirzah (Tell el-Far'ah North) later became an Israelite capital (1 Kings 15:33); Arad and Hormah lie in the Negev; Adullam is where David hid (1 Samuel 22:1). Some have lists of kings or rulers in the Amarna letters (Megiddo, Gezer, Lachish, Jerusalem, Hazor, Achshaph), which fits a land of many small city-states, each with its "king." Others, like Geder, Hepher and Lasharon, are hard to locate. "Lasharon" may be a misreading of "of the Sharon," naming the region of the king of Aphek; the Septuagint joins the two into one king (see the variant at 12:24).
